For those of you DBB sickos who care, I’m officially a married man! We had a spooky wedding on Halloween night and spent the past week in Cabo San Lucas for our honeymoon. We had a great time celebrating over the past week and a half!

Now we’re back to Pistons hoops.

JB Bickerstaff decided to mix up the starting lineup by starting John Collins at center. Paul Reed moved to the bench, and Daniss Jenkins was inserted into the starting lineup. Detroit started small with Duncan Robinson at the 3 and Ausar Thompson at the 4.

It proved to be the right idea early, as Collins was the leading scorer for Detroit after the first quarter with nine points. The Wizards took a 32-31 lead heading into the second, behind 12 points from Trae Young and 11 from Anthony Davis.

Detroit struggled to have an answer defensively for AD, and this was another game where Detroit missed Jalen Duren’s physicality and inside presence. Davis had 30 points and eight rebounds at the halfway point while only missing one of his 11 attempts. The Pistons put up 37 points in the quarter with five different players scoring more than seven points. Collins led the way with 15, Duncan had 14, and Cade had 11 as Detroit held a 68-58 lead.

The third quarter was all about Daniss Jenkins. Cade picked up his fifth foul halfway through the third, and DJ took the reins. He made Trae Young look like a traffic cone on defense as Jenkins went on to score 13 in the quarter. He consistently attacked Young, and Young never stood a chance. Detroit continued to extend their lead as they were up 103-87 heading into the fourth.

The fourth quarter was highlighted by two beautiful plays by Ebuka Okorie and Ausar Thompson.

First, watch Ausar find Okorie in transition as Okorie does his best Kyrie Irving impression:

AUSAR TO EBUKA WE ARE IN HEAVEN pic.twitter.com/jggv5WFEeC
— Rip Haminkton (@RedAlternates) November 10, 2026

Second, the Human Swiss Army knife blocks the 7-footer Alex Sarr on one end, then follows that up by directing traffic and finding an open DJ with a great bounce pass for a wide-open dunk:

Just let Ausar do everything pic.twitter.com/3nlVa0IHKi
— Rip Haminkton (@RedAlternates) November 10, 2026

The Pistons will continue to hope for a speedy recovery for Jalen Duren as they needed his inside physicality against Anthony Davis, who finished with 44 points and 13 rebounds while shooting 16-for-21 from the field. Detroit still managed to pull away with a 122-111 win behind three different players who scored 20+ points, despite none of them being Cade Cunningham.

John Collins, in his starting small-ball five role, led the way with 24 points and 10 rebounds, shooting 9-for-13 from the field. Both Daniss Jenkins and Duncan Robinson added 22 points each, and Jenkins led Detroit with eight assists. Your fun fact of the night: Robinson led the Pistons with seven free throw attempts. There has been a clear difference in his game this year as he looks to get to the line more often. Cunningham added 17 points and seven assists.

The Pistons improve to 7-3 on the season. Detroit’s home-and-home matchup with the Wizards continues as the Pistons will travel to Washington for Round 2 on Thursday night.

Go Stones.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Lakers: Austin Reaves pulls a Doncic to beat Detroit
pistons.body:
DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 8: Austin Reaves #15 of the Los Angeles Lakers drives to the basket during the game against the Detroit Pistons on November 8, 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Brian Sevald/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Who needs Luka Doncic when you have the US equivalent from Newark, Arkansas, Austin Reaves? The Los Angeles Lakers guard scored a game-high 43 as his MVP-level teammate rested with a back injury, propelling LA past the Detroit Pistons 121-116.

Honestly, the game had no reason to be as close as it was in the end. The Lakers led 40-14 one basket into the second quarter courtesy of insane shotmaking (hitting 72% from the floor) and an insane amount of Pistons miscues, including having more turnovers (eight) than made baskets (six).

But the Pistons, being the Pistons, weren’t about to give up. While Detroit pulled within one point early in the fourth quarter, the Lakers led wire to wire. So while it was only marginally competitive from Detroit’s point of view, it was certainly an instructive game. Here are some of the things I learned:

1. Kevin Huerter

Kevin Huerter is going to be a critical component of the Pistons’ rotation this season. In a game where Detroit’s entire backcourt didn’t really show up to play (both Cade Cunningham and Duncan Robinson were largely no-shows until some fourth-quarter scoring), Huerter was by far the biggest bright spot for the Pistons.

It also happened to be his best game in a Detroit uniform. Huerter hit four three-pointers, scored 24 points overall, and added five rebounds, five assists, five blocks(?!) and two steals. Ever since the Pistons traded for him at the deadline last season, it was clear Huerter makes winning plays, and you were hoping he’d be able to combine that with rediscovering his 3-point shooting stroke from earlier in his career. The early returns indicate the shot might be back, as well as everything that goes with it. After tonight, he’s hitting 40% from deep this season.

2. John Collins and Paul Reed

Detroit’s starting front court simply does not work, and it will never work. For as long as Jalen Duren remains sidelined or off the floor this season, this is going to be a significant issue for the Pistons. Duren is ramping back up from a hamstring injury and will be out two more weeks. Detroit has been, and will continue to be able to weather that storm. But it ain’t pretty, and any additional time off from Duren will have me significantly worried.

Most will want to pin the blame on the newcomer John Collins, and he has certainly played worse than Reed, but I think it’s the combination that brings out the worst in both players. Each is the kind of big man that relies on the gravity from teammates that allows them to use their athleticism to create the chaos that makes them effective. With both of them on the floor, it’s two bouncy balls pinging around the floor with no semblance of a plan on how to actually get the ball to the rim. The defense is also bad, and the rebounding is even worse. It’s an ugly situation, and it was exacerbated tonight by both men getting out-physicaled by the behemoth seven-footer Walker Kessler. Kessler, the Lakers’ big offseason addition, had 12 points and 16 rebounds, including seven on the offensive end. The Lakers also dominated the Pistons in the paint, 58-46.

Again, the lion’s share of the blame goes to Collins. He’s been quite bad all season, and it’s getting less clear by the day how he’s going to turn it around and be a positive force for the Pistons. I don’t think he’s ever met a 50-50 ball he couldn’t surrender to the opposition. But the pathway to him playing well lies with sharing the floor with Duren. Get well soon, JD.

3. Austin Reaves

The Pistons were correct in trying to give Austin Reaves the bag this offseason. Detroit reportedly was ready to give the wing a max contract this offseason as the second scorer and potential missing piece in a Detroit Pistons title run. Once the Lakers believed the pending RFA had a max offer on the table, they quickly moved to get an agreement to sign him on the eve of free agency so he’d never hit the market.

Reaves was insane tonight. The degree of difficulty on his shots begged belief. He was able to create space, get balanced, and score at all three levels. It was a sight to behold, and he was by far the best player on the floor for either team tonight.

4. Daniss Jenkins

Daniss has that dog in him, especially under two scenarios: 1. There is an impending buzzer. 2. He feels like his team is getting punked. Jenkins was truly the other hero of the game behind Huerter. He hit yet another buzzer-beater tonight, and he scored a career-high 31 points. When the Pistons were down huge, Jenkins got that look in his eye, as if to say, “This is not going to happen.”

From there, Jenkins started firing away from deep, and he was hitting. In the end, he canned eight three-pointers. He was also the ONLY Pistons player to go to the free-throw line more than once in the game. Really, Jenkins is like a better version of Marcus Sasser. He’s got scoring in his blood, and he’s more of an off-guard than a point guard, despite being stuck in a point guard’s body. He’s got three inches on Sasser and better floor vision, so he’s better overall and can cosplay as a point guard better than Sass, but Jenkins works best in this Pistons lineup when he’s not running the offense.

4. The refs.

The referees love the Lakers. Nothing else needs to be said.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs Lakers preview: Best Defense vs best offense
pistons.body:
Does it get any better than the No. 1 offense versus the No. 1 defense? The Detroit Pistons find themselves in that matchup as the 122-point-per-game Los Angeles Lakers visit Motown tonight.

Luka Dončić and the Lakers put up plenty of buckets, but scoring on Detroit is still an impossible task. The Pistons only surrender 101 points a game. Smothering defense every night.

Detroit’s defense has its biggest test of the season if Dončić suits up this evening. He’s questionable with lower back tightness.

It would be a shame if we’re robbed of Cade Cunningham going head-to-head with another MVP candidate. The bigger shame would be if we miss out on Dončić versus Ausar Thompson. That matchup is like Jerry Rice versus Deion Sanders with how both are operating.

GAME VITALS

Where: Little Caesars Arena, Detroit, MI

When: 6 PM EST

Watch: TV20 Detroit/DAZN-DET

Odds: Pistons (-4.5)

Analysis

Detroit hasn’t played since Wednesday’s loss to the Philadelphia 76ers. They’ve had plenty of time to rest up. They’ll need it if Dončić suits up.

Dončić is averaging 40 points. He’s shooting 42% on nearly 14 3s a game. He gets to the line more than anybody. It’s basically no stopping Dončić at the moment. This is a Wilt Chamberlain-like hot streak. Those two are the only players to average 40 nine games into the season. Whew, to say he’s balling is an understatement.

But tasks like this are why the Pistons employ Ausar Thompson. If *anybody* can slow Dončić down, it’s the best perimeter defender on the planet. Dončić usually has success against quick defenders with wiry strength, but Ausar is bigger and stronger this season. We’ll be keeping tabs on how Ausar takes Dončić’s bumps tonight. Ausar has the quick hands to disrupt things as well.

This might be a game where we see Paul Reed getting to the level and blitzing a bunch. J.B. Bickerstaff may decide to get the ball out of Dončić’s hands and force someone else to beat them. Reed is capable of coming to the level on screens and muddying things up.

I’m sure Dončić will see some Cade tonight too. Cade won’t make it easy with his sturdy frame. On the other end, the Lakers only have a few perimeter defenders to throw at Cade.

Matisse Thybulle is firmly in LA’s rotation as he’s started all 10 games. He’s still a defensive playmaking threat. Cade deals with defenders like this nightly, but Thybulle is a plus defender nonetheless. So is Ziaire Williams. The springy 25-year-old treats every possession as if he’ll never get in the game again if he doesn’t go hard.

Those two are solid defensively, and Jake LaRavia competes. Outside of that, Detroit will have plenty of favorable matchups (Walker Kessler is a great rim protector and is off to a good offensive start. He can make a difference).

Dončić displays effort and is trying to shake the terrible defender narrative on his name, but attacking him is still the best way to slow him down. Make him work and keep him involved in actions.

Austin Reaves falls into the same boat. He’s under Dončić on the Lakers’ best defenders on the team list. Anybody with that matchup should look to be aggressive.

Reaves spends most of his time covering shooting guards. Will JJ Redick make Reaves chase Duncan Robinson all night? That’s probably not ideal. Robinson runs even great defenders into the ground.

Robinson’s light-em-up stretch continues as he’s fourth in 3s made (35). Only Dončić, Nickeil Alexander-Walker, and Steph Curry have made more.

Detroit is letting it fly from deep as a team. According to Cleaning the Glass, 40 percent of their shots are coming from 3 (15th) compared to 31 percent last year (29th). Their rim rate has flipped the other way, but getting Jalen Duren back should rectify that.

The best offense versus the best defense is a mandatory viewing appointment. Can Ausar slow down the MVP-favorite? Do the Pistons show why they’re an elite defense and smother Dončić as a team? Does Cade deliver a masterclass against a guy he’ll be compared to for the foreseeable future if he’s in the MVP race? We’ll find out at 6 PM. Be there!

Projected starting lineup

Detroit Pistons (6-2): Cade Cunningham, Duncan Robinson, Ausar Thompson, John Collins, Paul Reed

Los Angeles Lakers (8-2): Luka Dončić, Austin Reaves, Matisse Thybulle, Jake LaRavia, Walker Kessler

pistons.headline: The Pistons go from owning to getting owned in the paint
pistons.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 04: Jalen Duren #0 of the Detroit Pistons looks on from the bench during a game against the Philadelphia 76ers at Little Caesars Arena on November 04, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

During a tumultuous playoff run and a prolonged offseason contract negotiation, Detroit Pistons fans were ready to say goodbye to Jalen Duren. Well, Duren has been out for six of eight games, and it turns out that Duren is the most indispensable member of the Pistons aside from Cade Cunningham.

A hamstring strain has knocked Duren out for six straight and counting, and boy, do you feel that every moment of every Pistons game.

Pundits and fans alike had easy diagnoses for what ailed the 60-win team during a disappointing second-round exit last season. Detroit needed a second scorer and much more perimeter shooting to succeed in the postseason. Its second-best player, the All-NBA big man Duren, couldn’t effectively operate in a congested, constipated offense when opponents had so much extra time to prepare their defense. That had a trickle-down effect on Cade Cunningham and on offensively limited players the Pistons relied on, like Ausar Thompson, Javonte Green, and Ron Holland.

This offseason, the Pistons seemingly tried and failed to add their second scorer (a planned run at Austin Reaves fizzled, and trade interest in players such as Kyrie Irving and Kevin Durant went nowhere). But they certainly addressed the team’s lack of perimeter punch. Detroit added guys such as Isaiah Joe, John Collins, and Taurean Prince. They re-signed midseason acquisition Kevin Huerter. They reformulated their offensive game plan to create more movement, space, and offensive responsibility among their non-Cade players. So far this season, the perimeter offense has hummed. Detroit is a top-10 team in 3-point shooting and almost middle of the pack in attempts despite Isaiah Joe missing most of the season to injury.

Detroit is 6-2, losing to the New York Knicks and on Wednesday night to the East-leading Philadelphia 76ers. Calls after both games from fans and casual watchers immediately turn to the team’s lack of that second star as the biggest issue. While that still might be a deal-breaker in the players, I would argue that the actual biggest issue in the season’s first eight games is Detroit’s collapse in its former ability to absolutely own the paint.

In other words, it’s not the lack of a Kyrie or a Durant or a Devin Booker. It’s the lack of Duren.

Last season, Detroit led the NBA in points in the paint, mostly behind Duren’s elite rim gravity and chemistry with Cade Cunningham and Detroit’s other ball handlers. Last season, the Pistons led the NBA with 57.9 points in the paint and were fourth in opponents’ paint scoring. They had a scoring differential inside of 14.2 points per game.  This season, Detroit ranks just 22nd in the paint at 44.8, down 13.1 points per game.

Rim gravity, it turns out, is just as important as perimeter shooting in creating the space needed to run a successful offense.

Paul Reed is a dynamic scorer inside, and he has some pop to his game. But he isn’t a rim runner like Duren. You give it to him on the block, and you let him work his magic. John Collins is opportunistic in transition, but those opportunities are dried up when he is the only big on the floor applying rim pressure, usually trying to duck in from the corners.

Ausar has the ball in his hands more, and it is working to create opportunities from others on the perimeter, but it is taking away a lot of those dunker-spot opportunities and back cuts that Thompson feasted on last season.

The lack of inside pressure is manifesting in other ways. Detroit has gone from a top-5 team in second-chance points to 22nd. They are 28th in offensive rebounding. Last season, they were third.

This team needs Jalen Duren back ASAP. And I think fans need to start reckoning with how crucial he is for this team to succeed.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs 76ers final score: Detroit falls short in East battle
pistons.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 04: Cade Cunningham #2 of the Detroit Pistons drives around Vj Edgecombe #77 of the Philadelphia 76ers during the first half at Little Caesars Arena on November 04, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Pistons (6-2) fall short in the battle between the top teams in the Eastern Conference. The Philadelphia 76ers (8-1) outlasted Detroit 112-106. Philly got up by as many as 18 points, but Detroit never truly went away. The 76ers’ stardom showed its head tonight.

After holding Jaylen Brown to 16 points in the first meeting of the season, he surpassed that in the first half this time around. Brown poured in 30 points for the game while converting on 11 of his 19 shots. He rained in spot-up 3s, as it was tough to stick with him with the way Philly forced Detroit into scramble mode throughout the ballgame. Brown had a clutch block on Cade, and his presence was felt on both sides of the ball.

This is not 2023 Joel Embiid, but he’s still a force. Embiid still draws double teams and can get any big in foul trouble. He and Tolu Smith got into a dust-up that injected some life into Detroit, but Philly found a way to withstand every Detroit storm.

Duncan Robinson went on a few personal runs that seemed to turn the tide in Detroit’s favor. The sharpshooter went for 27 points and buried an unconscious seven triples. Robinson’s ability to look past the hands in his face to shoot the rock will pay dividends all season. It didn’t work out tonight, but Robinson is off to a different type of start as a sniper.

Cade Cunningham tried to put on his cape and emptied the clip. He couldn’t find it from deep but got good looks. He went for 26 points, 11 assists, and seven boards. lions.headline: For the Detroit Lions, ugly wins are a thing of beauty
lions.body:
Nov 8, 2026; Miami Gardens, Florida, USA; Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell celebrates with defensive back Brian Branch (32) after an interception during the second half against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Nathan Ray Seebeck-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Winning the ugly ones is just as important as the pretty ones—they count the same in the standings, after all—and that’s where the Detroit Lions need to keep pace with an NFC North that refuses to ease up. For yet another week, everyone in the Black and Blue division with a quarterback capable of performing the forward pass picked up wins. It’s maddening, it’s odds-defying, it feels like it has to let up at some point, but until it does, winning is all that matters for this Lions team.

Most of the noise on game day centered on the new guy at left guard, Miles Frazier, stepping in for starter Christian Mahogany. In real time, people scrambled to find an explanation. Was Mahogany hurt in pregame warmups? What were his PFF grades over the last three games? Did he catch the South Beach Flu? People hardly had enough time to investigate before Detroit took the field and mustered up a measly 110 yards and six points on offense in the first half. Prior to halftime, fans had lost their patience with Frazier’s performance. Jared Goff was sacked three times, Jahmyr Gibbs had four carries of zero or negative yards, and the Lions were up just three points at halftime against a 1-6 Miami Dolphins team.

Enough was enough: Mahogany needed to be put in at left guard to help the Lions offense get back on track.

Except that didn’t happen. Mahogany played just five snaps on Sunday in Miami, all of those opportunities coming on field goal kicks. The Lions offense turned things around just enough in the second half. Goff stayed upright, Gibbs broke into the end zone for the game’s only touchdown, and the Lions defense (!) made sure this one ended in a victory. Not for them, but for their leader, Jack Campbell, who had to watch his defense from a hospital room, still regaining his physical faculties—but determined to return to the field.

Social media was filled with videos and photos of the Honolulu Blue takeover at Hard Rock Stadium, fans chanting and holding signs in support of Campbell and the Lions. Your feed was filled with as much love and support as it was with people wondering how Mahogany’s crime could justify the time he spent on the sideline. Dan Campbell offered no further insight into the infraction immediately after the game, but has since alluded to the fact that Mahogany had broken team rules “multiple times.”

Dan Campbell made the right decision when it came to holding Mahogany accountable. There’s no room in their building for anyone to be above the standard, whether you’re a starter or a healthy inactive on game day. That isn’t a new sentiment—it’s been the foundation since the afternoon Campbell walked through the door.

“But I’ll guarantee you this: these guys are gonna fight, and they’re gonna scratch and claw, and they’re gonna be something this city is proud of because they’re going to take on the identity of this city,” Campbell said in his introductory press conference.

“It ain’t always going to be roses up here. ‘Everything’s gonna be the way that we all want it to be and look perfect,’ but I know this, man, we’re gonna fight, we’re gonna scratch, and we’re gonna claw, and I know the good teams find a way to get it done.”

Campbell told us it wasn’t always going to be pretty, and we’ve been reminded over these past couple of weeks just how ugly football can get, but there’s something beautiful in it all.

“If somebody goes down, the next one steps up, and he’s expected to produce enough to help those guys next to him when these guys are going to learn to play together, play for one another.”

From the disciplinary action against Mahogany to Jack Campbell’s absence in the middle of Detroit’s defense, from the offense’s struggles to Kelvin Sheppard’s unit getting the job done, Sunday was a testament to how they’ve become that good team Campbell referenced over five years ago. Their 6-2 record is a reflection of the image this football team was built on by Dan Campbell.

“It’s not about the best 53, it’s about the right 53.”

lions.headline: NFL Week 10 power rankings: Despite 4 straight wins, Detroit Lions sit behind NFC North rivals
lions.body:
Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell watches a play Miami Dolphins during the second half at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The Detroit Lions (6-2) have now won four in a row, are 2-0 in the division with wins over the Packers and Vikings, and sit in second place in the NFC North, just a half-game back of the Chicago Bears. For the first time this season, the Lions rank in the top 10 of every national power ranking that we track.

But it’s not all sunshine and roses in the Lions’ relationship with the national media. Of the eight rankings we track, the Lions dropped this week in over half of them. Even more surprising, they dropped behind the Packers in two (Yahoo Sports and Sports Illustrated) and remain behind the Vikings in two others (Sporting News and ESPN)—despite having the same (Vikings) or better (Packers) record—and winning both head-to-head matchups.

Let’s take a closer look at this week’s national power rankings.

Sports Illustrated: 6 (Previous rank: 4)

From Connor Orr:

Having spent time in Buffalo after Damar Hamlin’s near-death experience in a Bills-Bengals game, I can still only begin to fathom the heaviness this Lions team is dealing with on a daily basis in the aftermath of the Jack Campbell injury. It makes the Dolphins victory feel very different… and somehow more amazing.

USA Today: 6 (Previous rank: 7)

From Nate Davis:

WR Amon-Ra St. Brown hasn’t scored since September and only has two 100-yard receiving games this season. Think the German-American star might break out Sunday in Munich − especially given how the Pats secondary just got shredded?

NFL.com: 7 (Previous rank: 5)

From Nick Shook:

Sunday’s victory wasn’t pretty by any means, but sometimes a team needs to find a way to win an ugly one. The Lions did that in Miami, getting just enough from Jahmyr Gibbs to leave with a W. That’s what I’d expect from a team in the top 10, but I’m hoping this was an informative experience to grow from, not a harbinger of things to come.

The Athletic: 8 (Previous rank: 7)

From Chad Graff and Josh Kendall:

It hasn’t always looked pretty (including in Miami on Sunday), and the underlying defensive stats (they rank 30th in EPA per play) remain concerning. But the offense has been among the game’s best as they now head abroad to face the reeling New England defense.

CBS Sports: 8 (Previous rank: 9)

From Pete Prisco:

It wasn’t pretty against the Dolphins, but they found a way. They can’t play that way this week against a wounded Patriots team or else.

Yahoo Sports: 9 (Previous rank: 8)

From Frank Schwab:

Is the Lions’ defense good? It has been better recently. For the third straight game the Lions’ opponent failed to top 17 points. Two of those games happened against the offensively challenged Vikings and Dolphins; the third game in that streak was against the Packers. Advanced metrics are kind to the Lions’ defense over the past three weeks too, as Detroit is eighth in EPA per play allowed and fifth in success rate allowed. Star safety Brian Branch returned from an Achilles injury three games ago, and it’s not a coincidence the Lions’ defense is much better with him back. The Lions have held opponents to 21 or fewer points in four straight games, the first time that has happened since 2016, according to the team’s site.

The Lions allowed just 228 yards and 12 first downs Sunday, and while that was against Miami, it’s still a lot better than Detroit looked on defense early in the season.

“We’ve cleaned a lot up,” Lions head coach Dan Campbell said, via the team’s site. “Guys are trusting what they’re being taught, they’re executing it and with that execution comes confidence.”

ESPN: 10 (Previous rank: 9)

From ESPN Staff, excerpt from Eric Woodyard:

International games are rare for the Lions, who haven’t played outside the U.S. since 2015. And this matchup in Munich is a homecoming of sorts for WR Amon-Ra St. Brown, whose mother is German and who has spent considerable time in the country. This contest also marks Detroit’s first game in Germany and the first time it is the designated home team for an international game, so this is certainly a huge deal. “You kind of need that extra story to tell,” NFL Germany GM Alexander Steinforth told ESPN. “You need that extra link into the market to have a really meaningful impact, and that’s Amon-Ra St. Brown.”

Sporting News: 10 (Previous rank: 11)

From Vinnie Iyer:

The Lions’ once-maligned defense has allowed only a total of 62 points during their four-game winning streak. They will get a good test against the Patriots in Munich, Germany, in Week 10, where Jared Goff needs to shake off back-to-back sub 200-yard, one-INT games.

lions.headline: Detroit Lions Kerby Joseph won’t play in Germany
lions.body:
Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph (31) looks on during warm up ahead of the New Orleans Saints game at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

On Tuesday morning, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell held his weekly interview with local sports radio station 97.1 The Ticket. When discussing the recovery progress of All-Pro safety Kerby Joseph, Campbell said that he doesn’t expect Joseph to be able to play in Week 10 against the New England Patriots in Germany.

“I’ll cut it out (the speculation). I don’t see him playing. I don’t see him playing in Germany,” Campbell told 97.1, per Will Burchfield.

Joseph injured his knee in 2025 during training camp, and limped through the first month of the season before succumbing to his injury. For just over a year, Joseph underwent rehabilitation, working to build strength in his knee. In late October, Joseph finally gained enough stability in his knee to start practicing once again and started his 21-day injury evaluation clock.

Over the last two weeks of practices, Joseph has slowly ramped up his participation levels, as he acclimates back to football activities. On Monday, Campbell said Joseph continues to make progress; they like where he is at and hope to get him even more involved this week.

“He did a good job last week, so we want to get him some more work.”

While Joseph is steadily improving, the early decision to keep him out of Sunday’s game overseas may seem premature, but for a player who hasn’t played in well over a year, it’s not unusual and shouldn’t necessarily be viewed as a negative regarding his progress. Campbell also noted on Monday, when discussing the trade for Andre Cisco, that he expected Joseph to return this season and would give the Lions’ secondary some flexibility.

“We get Kerby back eventually here. Kerby gives you flexibility, keep him where you need him or move him back and forth.“

The Lions don’t want to rush Joseph back into game action, but they are working against the injury evaluation clock, which expires on Tuesday, November 17. At that time, the Lions will need to activate Joseph to the active roster, or they can elect to keep him on the PUP list, which would end his season. If activated, Joseph could potentially return to the field in Week 11 when the Lions host the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

lions.headline: Discussion: What is your dream trade deadline move for the Detroit Lions?
lions.body:
PHILADELPHIA, PA - OCTOBER 18: Philadelphia Eagles linebacker Zack Baun (53) looks on after the game between the Carolina Panthers and Philadelphia Eagles on October 18, 2026 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Kyle Ross/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

Welcome to NFL trade deadline day. After 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, no more trades can be executed until the start of the league year in 2027.

For the Detroit Lions, that likely means this is their last opportunity to make a roster upgrade for the 2026 season. And while the Lions don’t have any massively pressing needs, they are in a bit of an arms race in the NFC. The Chicago Bears added DT Jeffery Simmons a couple of weeks ago. The Seattle Seahawks added guard Quenton Nelson. The 49ers brought back DeForest Buckner.

Detroit is in a good spot in the NFC—currently holding onto the fifth seed in the NFL playoff standings—but just about everyone in contention for a postseason spot is playing decent football right now.

The Lions have already made one minor move before the deadline, trading for reserve safety Andre Cisco. But I’m guessing most Lions fans want more. So today’s Question of the Day is:

What is your dream trade scenario for the Lions?

My answer: Trading for Eagles linebacker Zack Baun.

Philadelphia has already shown a willingness to trade amid their 2-7 start to the season. On Monday, they sent defensive tackle Jordan Davis to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a first-round pick and a future second-round pick. That’s a pretty penny to pay, and it may be indicative that Baun will be costly if the Eagles are going to let him go.

But in Baun, the Lions would be getting a dynamic playmaker. Baun does everything in that Eagles defense. He’s above average in coverage—grading 71.4 or better in each of the last three seasons, per PFF. He’s a pass-rushing threat, with nine sacks since 2024. And he’s an absolute force in the run game, as well.

He’d also come with an insanely team-friendly contract, seeing as most of his money is currently tied up in signing and option bonuses that stay with the Eagles upon a trade. Detroit would only be due a prorated version of his $1.215 million salary this year, then they would have an option for 2027 to pay Baun a $14.4 million option bonus to keep him around in 2027.

Now, that low salary would likely mean shelling out significant draft capital to lure him away from Philly. We’re likely talking about a second-round pick, minimum. But if that’s the price, I’d pull the trigger.

The Lions don’t just have questions at linebacker this year—with Jack Campbell’s future in football unknown, Jimmy Rolder on season-ending IR, and Devin White also on IR. But Detroit also has questions beyond this year. Only Campbell, Derrick Barnes, and Rolder are signed for 2027, and there’s an out in Barnes’ contract if Detroit wishes to move on. Baun would give the Lions a head start on fortifying their linebacker room for the future.

lions.headline: Teams interested in Sam LaPorta believe Lions want to ‘work out a long-term deal’
lions.body:
Mandatory Credit: Nathan Ray Seebeck-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

With the trade deadline looming, the Detroit Lions are reportedly getting calls about the potential availability of former All-Pro tight end Sam LaPorta. According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler, teams are under the impression that the Lions are not interested in making a deal, preferring to keep him and reach a long-term contract extension.

The Lions have received calls on TE Sam LaPorta, but teams have gotten the impression that Detroit would like to keep him and try to work out a long-terms deal eventually. pic.twitter.com/1OYQbcqq1U
— Jeremy Fowler (@JFowlerESPN) November 9, 2026

LaPorta is in the final year of his rookie contract, and both he and the team have been open about wanting to sign an extension. Unfortunately, reports have surfaced that the team and LaPorta’s agent have reached a stalemate, leading to some very public venting of frustration from LaPorta.

“I think the combination of getting your heartstrings twisted as well as the violent sport we play—it sucks,” LaPorta said on the Pardon My Take Podcast. “It’s disappointing that you go out there every week and you bear the risk of getting hurt. Like last year, whatever it was, Week 9, Week 10, I break my (expletive) back for this team. And then I’m going out there this year, and I’m ballin’, and maybe they’re just not showing the love.”

LaPorta spoke with the media just days after the podcast aired, wanting to add further context to his appearance.

“I guess I wouldn’t expect anybody else to really even care, but, emotionally, for me and my family, it’s an important thing for us. We want to have stability,” LaPorta explained. “We’re excited; in the upcoming months, we’re going to have our first kid, me and my wife. We’re going to welcome our baby girl into the world in Metro Detroit. We want to be here with the Lions.

“And I guess I’m getting emotional about it, but in the grand scheme of things, it’s really a business. And you have to respect what the front office is doing, because they’re the ones calling the shots. They’re the ones that brought me in. It’s my first team. They’ve been nothing but supportive of me and my career.”

Lions coach Dan Campbell insists LaPorta’s contract situation—and his comments—hasn’t distracted the team because they know who he is as a person and teammate, but Campbell didn’t directly address the situation or the team’s desires beyond the playing field.

General manager Brad Holmes has previously expressed a desire to reach a long-term deal with LaPorta, but has yet to address the media since reports of stalled negotiations. While not definitive, this report from Fowler suggests the Lions haven’t given up on getting a deal done.

lions.headline: Detroit Lions confirm Andre Cisco trade; still looking to see if ‘something else makes sense for us’
lions.body:
Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell, left, and general manager Brad Holmes walk off the field after practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The NFL trade deadline is set to expire on Tuesday, November 10, at 4 p.m. ET, and while the Detroit Lions have finalized a trade to acquire safety Andre Cisco from the New York Jets (and released tight end Jackson Meeks in a corresponding move), coach Dan Campbell said that general manager Brad Holmes “hasn’t stopped” exploring options to upgrade their roster.

While the Lions are getting healthier at safety—with the anticipated return of Kerby Joseph and potentially Thomas Harper—Cisco is a system fit, understands the team’s verbiage from his time with former Lions defensive coordinator turned Jets head coach Aaron Glenn, and helps upgrade the Lions’ secondary as a whole.

“We’ve liked Cisco from afar, having played against him and then even in free agency when he was at Jacksonville coming out,” Campbell said. “So, he’s athletic, he’s versatile. He knows our system. He knows the verbiage. So, we feel like this is a guy that can help us here a little bit. So yeah, we’re excited.”

Beyond the talent Cisco brings to the field, he also offers the Lions the flexibility to shift some of their existing players’ roles around, meaning a player like rookie Keith Abney, who switched to safety mid-season, could see his role expand back into some work in a more natural nickel role.

“Well, it gives us flexibility,” Campbell continued. “Cisco’s obviously played safety, played nickel. He can play other things on third down in your dime package. So can (Brian) Branch. We get Kerby (Joseph) back eventually here. Kerby gives you flexibility; keep him where you need him or move him back and forth. And then you mentioned Abney. Abney’s got flexibility now: nickel and safety. So, it does. It gives us flexibility, is what it does, and gives us depth too in some regard, wherever that happens at.”

As far as any other potential areas the Lions may want to upgrade, Campbell reiterated that Holmes is exploring options, but it needed to be the right fit at the right price:

“It’s about: is there a piece that could help upgrade us? Is there really, and what is it going to cost you? […] Doesn’t mean that we’re not still looking; see if there’s something else that makes sense for us. But our unit is playing pretty good football right now. [….] And so, it’s got to make sense for us, and it’s got to be something we feel like it can help us, or it gives us significant depth.”

lions.headline: Detroit Lions trade for veteran safety from Jets
lions.body:
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 4: Andre Cisco #8 of the New York Jets talks to teammates in a huddle prior to the game against the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field on October 4, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Lions are on the board for the 2026 NFL trade deadline.

According to ESPN’s Adam Schefter, the Lions are trading for New York Jets safety Andre Cisco. In return, the Lions are sending the Jets a 2028 sixth-round pick.

Cisco was drafted in the third round of the 2021 NFL Draft and spent the first four years of his career with the Jacksonville Jaguars. He played in 63 games for the Jaguars, starting 47 games for them over that time. After his rookie deal was up, he signed a one-year, $8.5 million deal with the Jets in 2025 and re-signed with the team on a one-year, $2.5 million deal this offseason.

This season, Cisco has seen his role diminished in New York after starting eight games for them last year. After starting the first three games for the Jets in 2026, Cisco has played a total of just 23 snaps with New York over the past five games.

In Detroit, Cisco should give the Lions some much-needed depth at the safety position. Brian Branch recent returned from his Achilles injury and Kerby Joseph could be on the path to returning now that his practice window has been opened up. However, the Lions have been struggling with their depth at the position. Veteran Chuck Clark has been the primary reserve and has played okay, tallying his second interception of the season on Sunday. But Christian Izien has been benched, Thomas Harper remains on injured reserve, and the Lions have scaled back the work of rookie Keith Abney, who moved to safety midseason. This move could open up the opportunity to move Abney back to nickel cornerback.

As for Cisco, he’s a versatile safety capable of playing both in the box and as a deep, coverage safety. He’ll be appealing to the Lions, because he’s an aggressive run defender. But he also has pretty good ball skills. In college, he tallied 13 interceptions for Syracuse, including seven in his freshman season. At the NFL level, Cisco has eight interceptions, 26 passes defended, four forced fumbles, and 2.5 sacks.

michigan.headline: Report: Michigan Football edge rusher Nate Marshall no longer with team

ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 24: Nate Marshall #94 of the Michigan Wolverines plays against the Indiana Hoosiers at Michigan Stadium on October 24, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Sophomore defensive end Nate Marshall is no longer with the Michigan football program and intends to enter the transfer portal, according to a report from Chris Balas of The Wolverine on Tuesday.

Marshall played a big role in Michigan’s defense early in the season after impressing during fall camp. He made 11 tackles, including 2.5 for a loss, and two sacks in 2026, including the game-ending sack in the win over Oklahoma. He played more sparingly as a freshman, appearing in 11 of Michigan’s games, mostly on special teams, and playing in just one game along the defensive line.

He originally came to Michigan as one of the bigger recruits in the 2025 class. The Chicago area native was listed as a high-four-star by various outlets, but never really played a big role for the defense aside from the first few games of this season.

It’s unclear what went into the decision for Marshall to no longer reportedly be with the team with three games still to go in the regular season. During fall camp, head coach Kyle Whittingham had remarked that Marshall had some off-field issues that were dealt with, but it’s unknown if this has played a role in Marshall no longer being with the team.

With the emergence of other players like Tariq Boney and Benny Patterson, though, Michigan has the depth right now to make up for Marshall’s loss in the interim. But one can imagine this will only be the start of some major roster changes, especially on defense, where Michigan is set to lose several starters to the NFL Draft and graduation this offseason.

Barner scores two different ways in Seattle

michigan.headline: Neck Sharpies: Insert Isolation
michigan.body:
Neck Sharpies: Insert Isolation

Seth
November 10th, 2026 at 1:46 PM

We need to pause today to do something extremely distasteful. We have to give credit to Michigan State football, specifically Pat Fitzgerald and Nick Sheridan's offensive gameplan against Jay Hill's defense. It wasn't subtle, and it scored no touchdowns despite starting most of their drives with excellent field position. But it's not like MSU had much going for them, with that awful WR room, their top three RBs out, a QB who isn't a run threat, and an unstable offensive line, on the road against a much more talented rival.
The reason I want to discuss it, as unpleasant as all this is to say, is I think MSU attacked a structural flaw in Jay Hill's defense. You don't get better if you don't know what you have to do better. And I guarantee this won't be the last team to do it.
And by "it" I mean Iso the ever-living f-word out of Michigan's defense.
[After THE JUMP: This is going to hurt, I'm sorry.]

ISO
...short for "Isolation," is just about the most simple offensive play you can run.
Step 1: Declare a MIKE.
Step 2: OL block the guys in front of you, leaving the MIKE for the Isolation blocker.
Step 3: Ballcarrier goes to whichever side of the Iso block the defender doesn't.
ISO
"Insert Iso" or "Insert" for short is a variation that just moves the Iso blocker's gap somewhere else. Insert is a slower-developing play, and more often comes with Inside Zone blocking rules that give the back options other than "Follow your fullback."
INSERT ISO

MSU ran a little bit of regular-ass Iso as well, but they mostly attacked Michigan with Insert.
Aficionados of Split Zone are probably saying that second example looks pretty familiar and yes, if you move this over one more gap and make the F's block a kickout you're running Split. Insert can even end up looking like Split Zone if the lead blocker is hunting for someone to hit and ends up kicking the guy outside. But Insert is not Split in one important aspect: the F's block is usually happening in the interior. The point isn't to shift blocks to a more advantageous angle; the point is to ram a fucking fullback into a fucking linebacker's face and run off the resulting collision.
Here is Michigan running Iso in happier times.

[link]
Here is MSU running Insert on the first play of the game on Saturday.

[link]
I don't think we need a detailed explanation because it's pretty obvious how this works just from watching the endzone angle. It's a gap play that looks like zone, MSU is comboing through the nose to Taylor to create one side of the gap. The other side of the gap is created by the RG vs Etta. The lead blocker is the TE, and the RB is responsible for going to whichever side of the lead vs MIKE block that Bowles isn't.

DEFENDING THIS
..is a matter of closing the gap and winning the block at the point of attack. Going back to my three-tiered formula on defense, you can win any play by doing one of three things:
Execute: Everybody does his job.

Dominate: One guy does a superb job.

Cheat (or "Scheme" if you prefer): Play rock-paper-scissors by calling something dangerous the offence could conceivably punish with a counter.

EXECUTION
The first clip above from Saturday shows Michigan trying to execute against this. Everyone had a gap they're defending. Bowles, as the MIKE, realizes he has to move the point of attack up to the line of scrimmage to constrict the RB's opportunity for vertical lanes to escape through.

He also chooses to get the TE's left shoulder because that is the wider gap that's forming. As much as Pierce has been wiped out by the combo down to Taylor, that space needs to have a defender in it. However that's not technically Bowles's gap; he's supposed to force the ball back to his help, which is Bracy, to our left and waiting up high.
When I grade LBs on their responses to Insert, I'm often looking for how much they rock back the lead blocker, and also whether they took the gap that was more dangerous, with consideration to where the help is coming from. When we talk about RPS with regard to how high the safeties are, this is a good example, because Bracy being 15 yards away from the POA is all space the offense gets to run in.
What happens then is Bowles uses his impact to push the TE as far back as possible and look like he's two-gapping while actually favoring the gap to our right (yellow) so the help can come down from our left.

That help is also in danger, since a WR is cracking Bracy from outside. The defense has an answer for that too: just as Bowles can spill to help, Bracy can make sure he stays inside that WR's block and spill to Hill, who is replacing the cracked guy. The result of the play, after all of that, is Hill tackling the RB—who tried to bounce outside again instead of using his downfield momentum—for a relatively short gain.

DOMINATING
Winning an Iso play with a singular effort is usually about defeating a block at the point of attack so thoroughly that the offense has essentially wasted that blocker. We can see that happen here with Lea'ea (DT #91):

[link]
MSU is tipping this play by shuffling the TE inside before the snap, which isn't a surprise since they've been running it a ton already by this point in the game and Michigan's only had moderate success at stopping it. At the snap this looks like the previous Inserts:

(Yes MSU has six linemen; they did that a lot too.)
Then Lea'ea swims around the right guard, who falls down.

Lea'ea then intercepts the lead blocker, who can't get to Bowles. Free LB in the hole means stuff city, or at least an opportunity for it since there's still plenty of space here for the RB to put on a move or run over the guy.

SCHEMING
...or cheating to stop Iso plays can be done in a lot of ways, which is part of the reason you don't see this offense very often anymore. One obvious response is to move a safety into box. Adding a box defender to the run fit creates a player the offense doesn't have a blocker for. When the lead blocker hits the MIKE, the MIKE takes one shoulder and the safety gets a free run on the other shoulder.

[link]
I feel like you don't need a breakdown of this, or the counter to it. Everyone plays safety-up/safety-down, to the point that even TV announcers, who except in certain cases (not Saturday's) think they're talking to utter morons, will often trust their viewers to understand that much. Another response, obviously, is to run blitz it. Again, I don't think you need this drawn up. It's unblocked linebackers in the backfield; you figure it out.
Another common way to snuff out Iso is—you guessed it—all about delivering defenders into the backfield to intercept the lead blocker before he's in any kind of position for the running back to cut off his block. The favored response is slanting, which shifts where defenders are while still maintaining a perfectly sound defense with a guy in every gap. Example:

[link]
MSU's setup looks pretty promising for an Insert up the gut, with Etta all the way in a 2-technique (heads up on the G) on one side of the gap, Lea'ea in a 3-technique (outside shoulder of the guard), meaning both A-gaps are clear for the insert to punch through.

The slant takes all of those gaps and goes "Just Kidding." Etta has slanted across the C to create a giant backup in the spot MSU wants to run, Staehling has inserted himself in the A-gap behind Etta's. The lead blocker has to stop and turn backwards to get to the MIKE (Bowles), which robs the Isolation blocker of any momentum he might have had for the RB to cut off of.

The running back can cut all the way back, robbing himself of his momentum, just to get to a gap Chris Bracy has had all of this time to fill. Or he can run into the gaps the DTs are occupying, which is typically the worst place to put the ball for physics reasons.
MSU had a counter prepared for this of course. Next time Michigan shifted their DT's block over a gap they had the lead blocker convert to a trap block while the

[link]

This may seem counterintuitive: you're blocking one guy with two, just the math when Lea'ea dominated. But because the MIKE is occupying an exterior gap he's essentially letting himself be blocked by the left guard while the LG is occupied with Etta.

When you cheat to something and get caught with a counter, you're usually giving up an explosive. In the conversation of playcalling, in general, it's a statement that this game of Rock, Paper, Scissors is over until the defense is willing to gamble for high stakes. You would rather
WHY DID THIS WORK AGAINST MICHIGAN?
I was extremely impressed with MSU's decision to rep Iso and stick with it for the duration of the game, because it accomplished a lot of their goals.
1. MICHIGAN HATES GETTING GROUND. Minnesota showed, by going under center and running three-yards-and-a-cloud-of-dust offense, that you can wear down Michigan's defense while avoiding its best parts. Things Jay Hill's defense is good at:
The secondary is (mostly) very old and talented, and unlikely to bust or give up anything in 1v1 situations.
Some of the defensive ends are dangerous pass-rushers (JHD seemed back, Nichols did not).
Their starting DTs are really tough to dislodge from the point of attack.
Things we knew were a little iffy going into the season:
Defensive tackle depth isn't great. Pierce and Etta are stars, though Pierce can only last so long. Lea'ea is a battler. After that they're weak.
The linebackers are small and generally not that good. Bowles has progressed magnificently this year but he's still very undersized. Staehling is just a guy—smart, but not a thunker like we hoped and middling in athleticism. Taylor is mistake-prone. NOB is young and small.
If you're looking for the best way to attack that defense, it's to run-run-run down the middle, challenging the DTs to stay on the field and the linebackers to make plays, and wearing out the safeties by making them have to play linebacker.
Iso went out of fashion in football because fullbacks running headlong into linebackers was pretty much solved by increasing the size of the defensive line until there weren't any gaps to squeeze through. Even with its starters on the field though, Jay Hill's defense tends to play light. Pierce is a stalwart, but Etta and Lea'ea are penetrators.
Once you get just enough room to fit a blocker through the gap you're attacking, the smallness of the Michigan defense—so good for their pass defense—becomes a negative. This example below is pretty canonical. Pierce is able to squeeze the gap shut some, but Etta is where he is, Bowles is thrown to the side despite his blitz, and Bracy, though he met the running back near the line of scrimmage, is 40 pounds lighter than the guy with a head of steam he's trying to bring down.

[link]
This play was Owusu-Boateng (#12) getting run well downfield by a 360-pound guard and Chase Taylor getting crumpled.

[link]
2. MICHIGAN STATE WAS WELL-SUITED FOR THIS. They actually have a decent offensive line, with a center who's a star and a left tackle who can move people in the run game. Their tight ends weren't very good as receivers but Sheridan was able to replace one with an offensive lineman and train another up for this game. Punching their rival in the mouth also had to appeal to Fitzgerald's sensibilities for the kind of team he wants to build in East Lansing, and the kid of statement he wants to make against Michigan, which is the #1 thing he's being graded on.
It also got them away from having to put those crappy receivers against Michigan's man-to-man cornerbacks, or subject their injured quarterback to too much abuse from Michigan's pass-rushers. You'll note whenever they had to pass, John Henry Daley was winning blocks (a couple of uncalled holds were the only reason he didn't have three or four sacks). Beating Michigan with the proper use of a Rhino must have been an extra twist of the knife.
And I have to say, MSU played by far their best game this season. You could tell they were feeling it at the end, their much-maligned tight ends and receivers, who got to crush rival face all night (see the last play linked).
Lastly it made use of the one thing they had in the backfield, which was a heavy back who would just have to follow his blocker. Versus more complicated runs like Power or Outside Zone, there isn't much to screw up as long as you run straight and don't fumble.
3. MICHIGAN'S OFFENSE SUCKS BUT HAS TALENT. From a holistic perspective, this comes back to Jason Beck in a way. The last thing an underdog wants—even with Jason Beck calling plays—is to give Michigan a hundred opportunities to throw deep to Buchanan or Marsh, or maybe finally one day break a big long run. Beck is a terrible playcaller who tends to want to get his cute shit called, but his offense moved the ball in previous games when it stuck to normal shit, and given enough opportunities there's enough talent to take a big chunk. Reducing the number of Michigan offensive plays increases the proportion of DAMMIT BECK calls and increases the likelihood of getting out of the Big House without a Buchanan Event.
Reducing the number of drives in the meat of the game also increases the value of things like Michigan running backwards on 3rd & 1 in going-for-it range and coming away with zero points. Michigan is only going to self-immolate so many times, however, so it's best to give them only six or seven real drives all game. The things they can do well, like Power or Duo, are only worth running when they have time to drive the length of the field, and their quarterback play has been so bad this year that giving them drives in 2-minute situations or late in the 4th quarter is (other than the one Hail Mary), usually pretty safe.
4. MICHIGAN'S DEFENSE IS STILL GOING TO GET YOU. For all the luck, strategic success, and hard-nosed winning MSU enjoyed on Saturday, Michigan did not give up a touchdown. This is not unusual for them. It's a really good defense, and the weaknesses referenced above are often hard to access. I'm not done charting the 4th quarter of this game but Jay Hill was able to dial up stuff late that he'd saved to book MSU off the field and give his team opportunities to win. There were sacks and interceptions left on the field, not to mention two MSU fumbles that the offense recovered. The big chunks MSU got were mostly uncharacteristic boners that can't usually be expected.
When playing a really good defense, you need to get what you can, and MSU's Iso strategy worked very well, retaining the ball for big chunks of the 2nd and 3rd quarters while playing a field position game that forced Michigan's offense to last long drives without a freshman quarterback, regressed offensive lineman, or dimwitted coordinator screwing it up. If they're only going to give you three yards per play, run something that's going to get you three yards consistently.
Michigan is going to need a response for this going forward. The defense played well enough that they still could have beaten a bad MSU team with an even half-competent offense, but that's not going to be the case against the defenses they have remaining on their schedule. The program is already at its lowest point since 1934; the few fans still watching aren't going to feel any better if they're just watching the other team shove winged helmets around.

michigan.headline: ‘Collaborative effort’ coming for Michigan Football’s offensive play calling
michigan.body:
Michigan offensive line coach Jim Harding walks out of the tunnel for warmup ahead of the game between Michigan and Penn State at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

After Michigan Football’s latest offensive meltdown — a mere six points to rival Michigan State during Saturday’s loss — the program has moved on from offensive coordinator Jason Beck.

Head coach Kyle Whittingham had plenty of good to say about Beck the human during his Inside Michigan Football radio show Monday night. However, like anyone who has watched the Wolverines’ offense this season, he acknowledged it was time for change.

“He’s a great person. He’s an excellent football coach. But for whatever reason, it just wasn’t clicking here at Michigan, man,” Whittingham said.

Now, offensive line coach Jim Harding takes over as the interim play caller. The early dismissal gives Michigan a head start on its search.

“We’ve already began a nationwide search for a coordinator. … Jim will hold down the fort, and he’s the assistant head coach, and in my opinion, was a logical guy to take over, and it’ll be a collaborative effort,” Whittingham said. “It’s not all on Jim. The offensive staff will obviously pitch in and help, just like always.”

Part of the offensive frustration comes from seeing it play so well the game prior at Rutgers. Freshman quarterback Tommy Carr seemed poised to take over QB1 duties for the rest of the campaign. Yet Carr looked … like a freshman in the MSU game, throwing for 138 yards and two interceptions.

Whittingham was noncommittal on the starter for this week’s game at Oregon.

“We will see,” Whittingham said. “That’ll be in-house until game time, and we will — it’s being formulated as we speak, over in the offensive staff room, and we will make that determination. Keep it under wraps until we trot one of them out there on game day.”

The staff has another decision to make with its kicker. Freshman Jacob Baggett missed his lone attempt against the Spartans — a 26-yarder — leaving further doubt at that position. It could mean more fourth-down attempts.

“It encourages you to be more aggressive on fourth down if you don’t have a feeling that you have a good, high chance to make the kick,” he said.

For all the offensive struggles, the defense held Michigan State touchdown-less. And despite probably a few too many yards after contact, the loss was once again not on them. Safeties coach Tyler Stockton is particularly grateful for the talent and depth at his disposal. That, combined with a room committed to growing, makes his life that much easier.

“It’s because they care about each other,” Stockton said. “They don’t want to let their teammates down. They don’t want to let each other down. And that really started off this summer, by us just doing certain things in our position room just to build the connection that they know, man. When the bullets are flying in, they’re gonna do whatever it takes to help the team out.”

Stockton called Chris Bracy, “a dog,” a “football player” and a “football junkie,” and has been more than pleased with how Mason Curtis has fit into the defense. Rod Moore remains the heartbeat of that unit, and despite the transfer portal era diminishing some rivalries, he embodies the passion for the Paul Bunyan Trophy.

“It’s been unbelievable to watch a kid just battle every single day for this program, to, every Saturday put his body on the line because he loves this place so much. I mean, it’s been a joy to coach him,” Stockton said. “I was frickin’ heartbroken on Saturday for that kid because he pours everything into this program.

Moore, who has dealt with his fair share of injuries, mostly seemed happy just to suit up with his teammates.

“I was dying to do it for the past two years and, finally, to get the chance to go out there and play game after game after game without second-guessing or having the doubt of, ‘Am I going to be able to play the next game?’ Feels good,” the three-time captain said.

Welcome to the Recruiting Roundup, our twice-per-week series breaking down the latest developments on the recruiting trail for the Michigan Wolverines. We’ll keep you up to date on the top targets, the visits they take, the predictions that analysts make, and everything in between. Here’s what you need to know today…

Michigan legacy recruit commits to Notre Dame

If it wasn’t bad enough that the Michigan football team suffered one of the most embarrassing losses in recent memory against rival Michigan State on Saturday night, the Wolverines also lost a legacy recruit to rival Notre Dame over the weekend.

BREAKING: Elite 2028 EDGE Asa Burch has Committed to Notre Dame, he tells me for @Rivals

The 6’5 225 EDGE chose the Fighting Irish over Michigan and Penn State

He’s ranked as a Top 40 Recruit in the 2028 Rivals300https://t.co/MfxIxtMmLb pic.twitter.com/8DKPlBq277
— Hayes Fawcett (@Hayesfawcett3) November 7, 2026

2028 four-star edge rusher Asa Burch chose Notre Dame over Michigan, announcing his commitment to the Fighting Irish on Saturday. Losing a recruit to a rival is always tough, but this one is even worse, as Burch’s father, Alfie Burch, was a defensive back at Michigan in the ‘90s. It was a tough weekend for the Wolverines.

Burch previously held Crystal Ball predictions in favor of the Wolverines after having visited numerous times throughout the course of his recruitment. Michigan could really use all the help it can get as it pertains to talent acquisition, so the recruitment of a legacy player like Burch shouldn’t have ended the way it did.

Burch is the No. 92 player in the 2028 recruiting class, and he attends Warren G. Harding High School in Warren, Ohio.

Michigan commit confirms commitment despite Texas push

Michigan landed a commitment from 2027 four-star defensive lineman Xaxier Muhammad back in May, but a recent push from Texas seemed to put said commitment up in the air a little bit.

However, Muhammad recently confirmed his pledge to the Wolverines is solid and will sign with Michigan during the early signing period on Dec. 2.

The next chapter begins! 💙💛

First and foremost, I want to thank God for every opportunity, every lesson, and everyone who has been part of my journey.

December 2nd, I’ll be making it official and signing with the UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN!

The work doesn’t stop here. Same… pic.twitter.com/bDAYTEwrkC
— Xavier Muhammad (@Xaviermuhamma24) November 9, 2026

This is great news, as there was a possibility that Muhammad would be taking another visit with the Texas Longhorns for their game next week. However, instead of that, he will be back in Ann Arbor when the Wolverines take on UCLA.

The Wolverines have a plethora of edge rushers in the class, but it’s been a struggle landing guys on the inside. With Muhammad being the only interior defensive line prospect in Michigan’s 2027 class, retaining his commitment is crucial.

Muhammad is the No. 112 player in his class and attends Shadow Creek High School in Houston, Texas.

Boise State commit has successful visit despite MSU loss

2027 three-star linebacker Ryce Palepoi was in Ann Arbor over the weekend to see Michigan host Michigan State. Palepoi committed to Boise State in June, but Michigan is now making a push and offered the Salt Lake City native over the weekend.

“This visit to Michigan really shook the whole game with my recruitment,” Palepoi told 247Sports’ Blair Angulo ($). “Meeting the staff and seeing everyone I knew from the Utah staff was so amazing and I have much love and respect for them. The highlight of the trip was meeting with all the coaches and getting to spend time with them. The in-person offer just means more — they showed me and my family such great hospitality and I am so grateful.”

The only positives from the game were on defense, and Palepoi had some good takeaways from that.

“Even with the game being a loss, the defense absolutely battled and they have straight dawgs all around,” he said. “Their linebacker play was off the charts, too. They have dawgs in that room and I really want to learn from older players like them. Michigan is right up there at the top of my list, but I want to take all my visits and use up the last amount of time to talk to my family and make sure I make the best decision for us.”

Despite the commitment to Boise State, it seems like Michigan has a solid chance at a flip here. Palepoi is the No. 1,505 player in his class and attends Corner Canyon High School.

msu.headline: Sun Finally Shines as MSU Downs Michigan in The Weather Report
msu.body:
ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 07: Nick Sharpe #52 of the Michigan State Spartans and the Michigan State Spartans mascot celebrate with the Paul Bunyan Trophy after a 15-6 win over the Michigan Wolverines at Michigan Stadium on November 07, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Holy expletive! Doth my eyes deceive me? Is this truly an MSU victory? Over the weasels? In their play pen? The answer is yes, yes to all of it. It has been a rough season without a doubt, but to beat Michigan, that is a game all of us would be happy to win. So, we finally have ourselves some real joy for this week’s weather report.

Sun #1

The first sun has to go to Joe Rossi. I mean the man barely has people available to take the field. The defense looked prepared, had a game plan, and executed. Five sacks, four turnovers and a near shutout all against your rival on the road without half of your normal starters is exactly why Rossi gets the sun. Plus the batted down passes, and tackle for losses just added to the reasoning. I loved the intensity and physicality of the defense. The defense has been gritty all year. Not always successful, but they’ve been gritty. They have had a grit that is what Spartan football is supposed to be. This was a special win and this defense deserves a lot of that credit. Now the question is, can a win like this give this team a push for the rest of the season?

Sun #2

My second sun is headed to the kicking game. First and foremost, Liam Boyd was lights out. Every kick mattered and he was as solid as someone could be. The 49 yarder, that could have been good for longer, was a nail in the coffin kick. Boyd wasn’t the only boot that made a difference. Rhys Dakin had some great punts. Only had to punt four times but three of them were inside the 20. That just allowed the defense more opportunity to tee up on the weasels. Let’s also not forget to give a shout out to Jacob Baggett for his beautiful doink off the upright. It was little things like that that gave me hope that we had a chance. Second time this season I’m handing out a sun to Liam Boyd.

Sun #3

I have a shared third sun. My first part is going to the stat sheet and MSU dominating in everything. Time of possession, passing, rushing, turnovers, and as usual against Michigan, penalties. It was a strange feeling to feel there was this chance all game long. Our memory of Northwestern and Illinois made it difficult to keep the hope but ultimately, MSU was in charge this whole game. Part two of this shared sun is going to the booing Michigan fans. There is nothing I love more that hearing weasel fans boo their own team, in their own house. Boo away Ann Arbor, boo your way through all your excuses.

Cloud #1

First cloud goes to the inability to punch it in the end zone. Michigan has a solid defense and one that showed that as it shut MSU out of the end zone for the whole game. MSU was close numerous times but never could cross the line. The Spartans have got to get the ball in the end zone when you get that close. Some of the problem was play calling and some was just being outplayed. Thankfully, MSU still managed to put points up with the field goals.

Cloud #2

Cloud 2 is headed to the 7 penalties because I can finally be a bit picky with the clouds. You have to expect the whistles when playing in the play pen and the 7 penalties were not good. Honestly though, it is hard to make this a cloud because MSU was playing physical and typically would have been called for even more. I’m glad they were getting hands on receivers and fortunate the interference calls or even phantom late hit calls weren’t called to benefit the weasels. So, this is like a half cloud, which leads me to my next conundrum.

Cloud #3…nah Sun #4

I’m sorry my friends but I am too elated to talk negative and my hatred for the opponent has been at unhealthy levels since childhood. So, let’s talk about some more sun. I want to mention some individuals who helped this win. Shout out to Alessio for getting on the field after being questionable all week. Shout out to Chrishon McCray for some big time catches to keep things moving and momentum staying with Sparta. Shout out to Brandon Tullis who had 25 carries for 86 yards. There were not many of those 86 yards that came easy, but he continued to push and at times get just enough. Lastly, a shout out to Coach Fitz. The final score has not always been in our favor but the grit, the handling of adversity, the effort being made to get back to what Spartan football is has been noticed. I know there are plenty that don’t want him here and hated the hire. I think after the way this team has fought each week through all of its adversities is a testament to your coach and I think Fitz deserves some credit for that and a bit of grace.

Well, let’s hear it TOC, I want to see those suns and clouds in the comments. Before you do though, can we just take a moment to breathe in, smile, give a little laugh that we managed to beat Michigan coming into the game on a 6 game losing streak? Please make sure you irritate every weasel you see this week, especially the Walmart ones, because even with the loaded excuses that are sure to pour out, Paul is still going to be back where he belongs. Go Green!

msu.headline: Instant Recap: Michigan State Takes Down um, 15-6
msu.body:
Nov 7, 2026; Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA; Michigan State Spartans wide receiver Chrishon McCray (13) runs the ball against the Michigan Wolverines at Michigan Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Rick Osentoski-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

From early on in this game, and as many people already knew, it was clear that this was a game between two not good teams.  Unfortunately for us Spartan fans, we have had a couple unlucky breaks while tonight’s opponent has had some good fortune in their season.  Watching the two teams in the first half, one would imagine their records were closer than the reality.

Michigan State got the ball first and moved the chains one time before punting.

On their first defensive stand, Michigan State got a turnover when safety Devin Vaught came down with a pick after a pass went off an um receiver’s finger tips.

Starting a yard inside um territory, the Spartans reached 4th & 2 on the first series.  Coach Fitzgerald decided to be aggressive, and the play call was for a deep shot.  Personally, I would have rather punted here to try pinning an unimpressive offense deep.  Predictably, the deep shot did not pay off.  Receiver Bryson Williams had a chance at it but dropped the pass.

The two teams traded punts on their next possessions, totaling 17 yards of offense between them.  On um’s ensuing drive, they had their best drive of the half, moving 71 yards in 13 plays over six and a half minutes.  They reached the MSU 7, but a 3rd & 1 run lost a yard and brought out the field goal unit.  The kick went off the near side upright and bounced out, keeping the game with no points on the board.

Again, the two teams traded punts.  Getting the ball right at the 50, the Spartans marched all the way to the 3-yard line before having to settle for a field goal, which Liam Boyd made.  Just like that, the Spartans were ahead.

MSU then forced a 3-and-out.  Chrishon McCray muffed the punt reception but retrieved the fumble, and MSU took over at their own 44.  MSU picked up a couple first downs, the second on a 35-yard pass to McCray that got the Spartans down to the 13.  A bogus offensive pass interference penalty in the endzone pushed MSU back near the 20 and eventually led to another FG try, which Boyd comfortably made.

There was only time for a kneel-down after the kickoff, and MSU took a 6-0 lead to the break.  Our defense only gave up 78 total yards through two quarters.

MSU started the second half on defense, and after giving up a first down on the first play, forced a punt.  Unfortunately for us, that punt was allowed to land and it flatlined at the 1-yard line, pinning Alessio Milivojevic and the MSU offense against the goalline.

Starting from the 1-yard line, Michigan State had, perhaps, their most impressive drive since week 2.  The Spartans held the ball for 10:41 of game clock, ran 17 plays, and picked up 6 first downs.  There were passes, runs, wildcats, and overall dominance from MSU.  After reaching the um 12, the offense finally came to a halt with a run for a loss and then a sack.  Liam Boyd came on and hit his 3rd field goal, this one from 38 yards, to put MSU up 9-0.

On um’s ensuing drive, the referees started trying to help the home team.  After it looked like MSU was going to force a 3-and-out, a penalty was called for “illegal substitution” because an MSU defender had the heel of his shoe still on the field when the ball was snapped.  So um got another crack at a 3rd down play, on which MSU was called for pass interference (after a called reception was overturned).  On the next play, um ran the ball through the middle of the Spartan defense, but Lafaele punched the ball out late and Nikai Martinez recovered the loose ball.  Of course, after the play, MSU was penalized 15 yards for celebrating.

After a 28-yard catch-and-run by Chrishon McCray, MSU went backwards for a few plays and ended up punting, but Rhys Dakin pinned um at their own 7 with 12:01 to play.

After giving up a first down to start the drive, the Spartan defense then tackled um for a loss of a yard on a running play, followed that up with a sack by Derrick Simmons, and then got an interception from NiJhay Burt on a deep shot at the MSU 38.

Back on offense, the highlight of the drive was a 36-yard play to Bryson Williams.  The drive lasted 10 plays and over 5 minutes of game clock, and ended in Boyd’s fourth field goal to put MSU up 12-0.

With just over 5 minutes left, um needed to do something quick.  Instead, they held the ball for two plays, fumbling at their 37-yard line after a catch.  NiJhay Burt forced and recovered the fumble.

The Spartans ran the ball three times, then brought Boyd on to hit a 49-yard kick for a 15-0 lead.

The MSU defense then forced a turnover on downs on the first series of um’s possession… but a pass interference gave um an extra life.  After two incompletions and an 11-yard sack, MSU surrendered a 22-yard pass on 4th down.  An 11-yard run moved the chains again for um.  Two plays later, they hit a 31-yard pass to the 1, and then scored a play later to ruin the Spartan shutout.  Now trailing 15-6, um elected to go for two, but Kenny Soares shut that down with an amazing spin move to get home for the sack.

The kickoff was an obvious onside attempt, but the ball only went 6 yards before hitting an um player, giving MSU the ball.  Three kneeldowns later, it was game over and VICTORY FOR MSU!!!!

Sure, it would have been even sweeter to get the shutout, but this was still a dominant win against our rival in a game no one, including myself and many here among TOC Nation, was really giving us much of a chance to win.  For the game, MSU outgained um 298-192 and controlled the clock with over 38 minutes of possession.  The defense created four turnovers.  As Pat Fitzgerald said after the game, “Paul Bunyan is coming home to East Lansing!”

While it can still be said that this was a game between two not good teams, it is clear that um is much more not good than MSU.
