tigers.headline: Kevin McGonigle named 2026  AL Rookie of the Year
tigers.body:
DETROIT, MI - SEPTEMBER 27: Kevin McGonigle #7 of the Detroit Tigers waves to the crowd during the game between the Pittsburgh Pirates and the Detroit Tigers at Comerica Park on Sunday, September 27, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Izzy Rincon/MLB Photos via Getty Images) | MLB Photos via Getty Images

He’s done it. After one of the better rookie seasons by a 21-year-old in the sport’s history, Detroit Tigers infielder Kevin McGonigle has been named the Jackie Robinson American League Rookie of the Year for 2026. He won the award with 28 of 30 first place votes. Guardians left-hander Parker Messick got the other two votes to finish second.

Despite skipping Triple-A and being one of the youngest players in the league, McGonigle served immediate notice on Opening Day, when he racked up four hits in a stellar major league debut. He went on to slash 278/.376/.430 with 18 home runs, 12 stolen bases, with nearly identical walk and strikeout rates. He posted a 129 wRC+ for the year while grading out as an above average shortstop and third baseman per defensive runs saved. His 5.4 fWAR was fourth in the American League, while his 7.1 rWAR was first in the American League and fourth in the major leagues. He’s just getting started.

The Detroit Tigers promoted McGonigle to the major league roster on March 24, 2026, ensuring that he would be eligible to earn the Tigers a Prospect Promotion Incentive (PPI) pick if he won Rookie of the Year, or if he finished top three in MVP voting over his first three seasons in the major leagues. By promoting him early, and then waiting until into the season to sign a 10-year extension, the Tigers both kept him eligible for the PPI pick and got him locked up for a decade. He cannot earn another PPI pick going forward.

The plan has come together perfectly, as McGonigle’s Rookie of the Year award earns the Tigers an extra draft pick in the 2027 amateur draft next July right after the first regular round. In addition, the Tigers will have roughly $3M added to their bonus pool in the draft. So on top of their normal first round pick, the Tigers will have the PPI pick, and then they’ll also have their Competitive Balance pick in the A round next summer, giving them three of the top 40 picks in the draft.

"Trying to find a routine that works best for me… that's what helped me this year, picking everyone's brain and getting as much help as I could."@tigers star Kevin McGonigle shares how he avoided the rookie wall on the way to winning AL Rookie of the Year! pic.twitter.com/nMlaaW3EXx
— MLB Network (@MLBNetwork) November 10, 2026

McGonigle’s skills and ongoing development, along with excellent poise and leadership ability for a player so young, all say this is just the beginning for him. The raw power to hit a lot more home runs is already present, and he has the hit tool to do it without selling out for power very often. He’s already tracking like a regular MVP award contender for many years to come, and Tigers fans are going to love watching him anchor the club for the next decade or more.

The Cleveland Guardians’ LHP Parker Messick was the runner-up, with Boston Red Sox lefty Peyton Tolle finishing third. Both made outstanding debuts, and Messick in particular finished strong enough to really challenge McGonigle in the voting, and made a good case for the AL Cy Young award, to be announced on Wednesday night at 7:00 p.m. ET, as well.

Congratulations to Kevin McGonigle on a truly special season that took a bit of the sting out of the Tigers’ failings as an organization this year. The best is yet to come.

tigers.headline: RHP Dustin May may fit the Tigers’ needs for starting pitching depth
tigers.body:
ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA - OCTOBER 27: Dustin May #21 of the Milwaukee Brewers throws a pitch during the first inning against the Tampa Bay Rays in game four of the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on October 27, 2026 in St Petersburg, Florida. (Photo by Carmen Mandato/Getty Images) | Getty Images

With the near certainty of a lockout and a long fight between players and owners this offseason, it’s hard to get real enthusiastic about free agency right now. It’s usually hard for Tigers’ fans in the first place. While there is the idea being floated that top free agent Tarik Skubal may sign before the December 1st lockout if the right offer is available, with the Dodgers, Mets, and Cubs, generally regarded as his main suitors, he’s a pretty unique case. Apart from Skubal, there seems to be widespread expectation that most free agents will wait until new terms of the next collective bargaining agreement are announced before signing. Likewise, teams need to know the payroll constraints they’ll be working under to really manage their budget for free agents.

However, there’s also likely to be a set of moves from many teams simply designed to shore up depth where possible before the lockout begins. Scott Harris has a habit of trying to add a depth starter early in the offseason. These moves have generally gone pretty poorly, although Drew Anderson was a better choice last year than most. Even so, Harris certainly seems to emphasize getting a little depth in his offseason shopping early on, perhaps with the idea that he won’t have to force a move later. This strategy has not worked out terribly well, but that’s more been a matter of picking the wrong pitchers. The theory is still reasonably sound, particularly with the lockout looming. I wouldn’t be surprised to see him try it again.

The Tigers have a pretty solid group to build a rotation out of next season, but they aren’t necessarily that deep either. By 2028 the Tigers may have a pretty good crop of starting pitching prospects in the upper minors. Right now, they do not. And as we’ve discussed repeatedly since the regular season ended, the Tigers need for high leverage relievers is best answered by converting 1-2 of their starters with big stuff, but limited recent workloads, into relief help. To do that they’re going to need to pick up another starting option this offseason.

The criteria is pretty simple. We’re just looking at short term deals here. The Tigers are highly unlikely to go after a big target in the starting pitching market. National media is going to continue to report that the Tigers are “keeping tabs” on the Tarik Skubal market, but no one is buying that as long as the reported price tag remains well over $300 million. The Tigers will be angling for depth here unless Scott Harris decides to break his usual patterns, so it’s not going to be a thrilling signing when and if they add an arm. Deciding to lock up a decidedly mediocre journeyman reliever in Jacob Waguespack should probably be seen as the corollary to any depth starter signing that could come before the lockout begins.

Let’s take a look at Dustin May, who is a pretty good all around fit for what the Tigers will probably look for in a free agent starter.

RHP Dustin May

SeasonIPERAFIPK%BB%HR/9fWAR2025132.14.964.8821.19.61.430.72026145.24.703.6323.28.10.862.8

This veteran right-hander makes some sense for the Tigers. The lanky 29-year-old has never been able to translate his velocity into high-end whiff rates, and his breaking stuff has never carved hitters up the way many expected when he was a prospect. On the other hand, he’s fairly consistent and took a notable leap in preventing home runs this season while finally putting his years in injury purgatory behind him.

Between 2021-2024, when he was still with the Dodgers, May’s career was in shambles as he had two UCL reconstruction surgeries with just a brief comeback in between them. He was still effective in his brief stints on the mound, but his early potential was going to waste as his mid-20’s were largely spent on the injured list. He was traded to the Boston Red Sox at the deadline in 2025. The Cardinals signed him to a one-year deal worth $12.5M for 2026 before they dealt him to the World Series champs back at the trade deadline. For two seasons now he’s been generally healthy, throwing 132.1 and 145.2 innings the past two seasons, with no major injury trouble.

May is still averaging just shy of 97 mph on his fourseam and sinker with a bit more than average extension. He’s largely backing that with his 93-94 mph cutter in a very fastball heavy profile. He uses his 86 mph sweeper a decent amount, but the break on that is a little too big to fool major league hitters as much as the movement might predict. May rips his 86 mph sweeper at over 3000 rpms, and late in the season, he started throwing more of a straight curveball at 83.7 mph, with the same monstrous spin rate and getting more whiffs with it. We didn’t see it working as effectively in the postseason. In general, May gets a very balanced spread of grounders, line drives, and fly balls, so he’s fairly neutral in terms of how park factors will affect him.

He still feels to me like a guy who might be better off ditching the cutter and trying to throw more of a prototypical slider instead, while continuing to experiment with the sweeper/curveball combo as more of a strike stealer that is hard to square up for lefties. Sometimes throwing cutters, fourseamers, and sinkers all can diminish each of those pitches individually by requiring some fairly subtle feel differences how they’re gripped and released.

However, May was with the Dodgers a long time, so I would guess there have been plenty of stuff experiments under smart coaches along the way. The intriguing note for me was his increased curveball usage late in the year and the velocity on that pitch. Both Jackson Jobe and Beau Brieske started ripping an 85-86 mph curveball that neither had really thrown before, and the pitch looked pretty whiffish in the brief looks we had of them. Possibly the Brewers were thinking along similar lines with May, making this a little more interesting fit in Detroit.

May intrigues me to a degree is that he’s missed a lot of time in his career and really hasn’t had long stretches of good health in which to actually hone his craft and get better. Of course, you can just as easily call that being injury prone, but you take a look at May’s raw stuff and the wildly varying arm angles from year to year, it feels like he’s still tinkering for the right arm angle and stuff.

The Tigers don’t really need a workhorse here. May just completed back-to-back full seasons for the first time in his major league career, and yet he’s been with four teams over those two seasons. He hasn’t had a chance to settle in anywhere. And yet, May had a pretty good first half before fading as the season progressed. His 4.38 ERA with the Cardinals was solid, and he boasted a 3.15 FIP in St. Louis that said he’d actually been somewhat unlucky. He dealt with back tightness in June and then an ankle contusion in July, and really wasn’t pitching well through that stretch.

May briefly got off to a good start in Milwaukee, but blew up in a start on August 19th and the next time out took a 106 mph liner to his back, striking him in the upper back on the right side. He struggled the rest of the way, posting an ERA of 5.65 with the Brewers as they limited his starts and kept a quick hook on him. He was okay in the postseason, but again was working short outings with a mix of starts and relief appearances after an opener.

May dominates right-handed hitters. His trouble has always been allowing power and walks to lefties. In 2026, the problem was really just those walks. The Tigers being in pretty good shape with lefty relievers says that May would have a quick hook hanging over him in the middle innings of any start where a tough pocket of lefties was coming up in the opposing lineup.

Things are set up pretty well for May to have a solid season in 2027. I wouldn’t expect much more than 125-145 innings, but his production should be basically league average or a little better. He would be the Tigers’ fifth starter, and might get flexed into middle relief work here and there as well. That would allow the Tigers to use one of River Ryan, Troy Melton, or Keider Montero in high leverage roles along with Drew Sommers and hopefully, Will Vest next year. If Reese Olson is finally healthy, that opens up more options.

I’m not convinced that May has tons of upside remaining or anything, but his velocity and ability to spin the baseball will continue to intrigue teams around the league. The Tigers would be happy with his Cardinals production during most of the 2026 season, and hope to help him be more consistent from start to start and cut down on the walks to lefties. Solid depth starter work with some flexibility would do just fine, though he’ll likely be angling for a two-year deal after proving that he’s finally beyond all the elbow troubles.

MLB Trade Rumors projects a two-year, $30M deal with a player opt-out after year one. Like most contracts of this type, you’re rarely going to love it, but it might be just what the Tigers need to allow them to focus on the bullpen.

tigers.body:
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 17: Manager A.J. Hinch #14 of the Detroit Tigers looks on against the Chicago White Sox at Rate Field on September 17, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Tigers confirmed recent reports on hirings for their 2027 coaching staff on Friday. They announced the hiring of Kyle Hudson as the new first base and baserunning coach. Hudson worked with outfielders in his most recent job as Boston Red Sox’s third base coach, so perhaps he’ll take on some of those responsibilities in Detroit as well. Still the emphasis from the Tigers is on the baserunning side. Hudson was also an assistant coach for the Cleveland Guardians from 2020-2022 before joining the Red Sox.

The Tigers had already hired longtime major league catcher Martin Maldonado, whom AJ Hinch worked with briefly in Houston, as their new quality coach this offseason. Maldonado was behind the plate during the Astros 2022 run to the World Series championship. He brings a strong reputation as a leader and game planner, as well as his skill coaching the position, to the Tigers.

Longtime catching coach Ryan Sienko, who joined the organization in 2021, AJ Hinch’s first year as manager, will retain his duties coaching catchers, but will also now handle duties as bullpen coach following Juan Nieves departure from the organization. It’s typically a pitching coach in that role, so that’s a bit interesting. Presumably, Maldonado will handle more of the pre-game pitch planning with Dillon Dingler and Eduardo Valencia, while Sienko will continue coaching the actual catching skills, but perhaps their responsibilities will be mixed between them as well.

The Tigers have yet to replace Gabe Ribas as director of pitching in the farm system after his departure to work for the Colorado Rockies last offseason. They’ve replaced Nieves, who has been Chris Fetter’s assistant pitching coach since 2021, with a catcher, leaving Fetter and assistant Robin Lund as a duo to coach the pitchers. Perhaps they’ll end up hiring a new pitching director this offseason, but it’s a bit peculiar that they’re cutting out both major and minor league pitching coaches. Those responsibilities still have to be fulfilled by someone, but without some detailed clarification from the organization it’s difficult to pin down who is actually doing what at this point in regard to those roles.

The Tigers have named Kyle Hudson as their major league first base and baserunning coach.

Martin Maldonado has been named major league quality coach.

Michael Brdar, Cody Asche, and Lance Zawadski, who seem set to be retained for 2027. Boyer was the Tigers quality control coach last season, and will cede that job to Maldonado.

Cody Stavenhagen of The Athletic also reports that the Tigers have hired Scott Peters as their new medical director, while Jeremiah Randle has been hired as the Tigers new athletic trainer. tigers.headline: Beau Ankeney mashed his way onto the prospect radar in 2026
tigers.body:
PHOENIX, AZ - MARCH 29: Beau Ankeney (35) Grand Canyon Infielder takes a big swing during a baseball game between the Arizona Wildcats and the Grand Canyon Lopes on March 29, 2022, at GCU Ballpark in Phoenix, AZ. (Photo by Zac BonDurant/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

There are two particular categories of player that go under the radar in the major league amateur draft each year. The first are college seniors. If you didn’t get drafted by your junior year or earlier, as a JUCO or prep player, there’s a natural stigma attached. The second are first basemen. Because the position is usually filled by less athletic players whose value is heavily tied up in their bat, only the top ranked college first baseman really get much notice, and they tend to go in the early rounds as some of the better hitters each year. Leaving aside the player and just considering the profile, Spencer Torkelson was a hard player to philosophically wrap one’s head around as the first overall pick in the draft back in 2020. Living up to that would’ve required him to develop quickly into one of the better hitters in baseball. There’s a reason you very rarely see a 1-1 first baseman.

Detroit Tigers prospect Beau Ankeney checks both boxes, and he definitely didn’t get much attention on draft day 2025 when they picked him in the 14th round out of Loyola Marymount and paid him just the minimum signing bonus. He played three years at Grand Canyon University before breaking out and transferring to Loyola for his senior season in 2025. That was notable, as he was clearly a bit of a late bloomer. Also notable was his muscular six-foot-three, 235 pound frame. He only played in four games after the draft, so there wasn’t anything to get excited about yet. That changed in 2026.

Ankeney mashed 24 home runs total, including 9 in just 27 games at the High-A level after he was promoted in late July. He took his walks. He showed pretty good athleticism for a first baseman, with enough speed to handle a corner outfield spot here and there. His raw power really stood out, as he averaged 92 mph off the bat, which is great even at the MLB level, and maxed out at 114.4 mph off the bat, giving him a 65 FV grade on his raw power potential. And most importantly, he took his walks and didn’t strike out that much for a power hitter.

In Lakeland at Single-A, Ankeney chased about 30 percent of the time, and his whiff rate was similarly on the higher end of the scale. Considering that he was 23 years old already and competing with 19-22 year old players quite a bit, it was impressive, but didn’t really knock anyone’s socks off. What really got prospect hounds talking was the fact that he went straight into High-A and did even more damage, without much of an increase in his strikeout rate. From August 4 through the 16th, Ankeney hit seven homers in nine games while walking and racking up one multi-hit game after another. He was the hottest hitter in the league for that stretch before cooling down over the final weeks of the season.

Beau Ankeney is on an all-time heater. He crushes another homer here to put the Whitecaps up 5-3. It’s his 2nd of the game, his 5th in his last 5 games, and his 7th in 14 games at High-A. Sheesh. @ThatDanHasty calls it. pic.twitter.com/TK36VMUrD6
— Tigers ML Report (@tigersMLreport) August 15, 2026

He does chase too much right now, and there’s some swing and miss in his game, producing at 24.3 percent K-rate in Single-A, and 27.5 percent in High-A, but that’s not terrible either. He also showed nice feel at times for hitting the ball where it’s pitched, driving fastballs away to right field with authority, and hitting tape measure shots to center and left-center when he got something middle or middle-in over the plate. He hits from an upright stance and is pretty flat through the hitting zone, making him strong against the high fastball. He can get some tilt to launch sinkers and secondary pitches that hang up in the zone as well, but a pitcher that pounds the bottom rail can give him trouble. Still, it’s a compact inside-out move that works to the big part of the field pretty well as long as he doesn’t get too pull happy. He struggled some with breaking stuff and that will be something to watch as the pitching he’s facing gets tougher, but he hit for average and plenty of power against fastballs and offspeed stuff.

Obviously there’s a caveat here due to his age. He’s a little older and more physically mature than a lot of the pitchers he faced this season. The short sample in the Midwest League to close out the season was really impressive though, and lends credence to the idea that he was putting it together nicely late in his first pro season. Another plus for him is the athleticism, in that he isn’t the typical big hitting statue you typically find in a college first baseman.

I’m not going to get too carried away just yet, but it’s good to see another power-hitting right-handed bat with potential in the system. Hopefully we’ll see him refine his approach and start to handle the nastier stuff he’s seeing at the High-A level more consistently next season. He’s probably never going to be a high contact hitter and there’s certainly risk in the hit tool, but the fact that he sprays the ball around is pretty promising for his future batting average projections. So is the batspeed and hard contact he’s mustering.

Beau Ankeney wasn’t the biggest breakout prospect of the year for the Tigers, but he was among the least expected and should feel great about his full season debut. No doubt the Tigers do.

tigers.headline: Detroit Tigers 2026 BYB preseason prospect list review #21-30
tigers.body:
Detroit Tigers catcher Eduardo Valencia (32) is interviewed after helping bring in the win against the Pittsburgh Pirates at Comerica Park in Detroit on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

This is installment three of our look back at the 2026 BYB preseason prospect rankings and scouting reports for the Detroit Tigers. Typically, we don’t revisit each prospect on our rankings until we re-grade them for next year’s reports and rankings in the leadup to spring training. This year, with a potentially much longer offseason while the CBA negotiations go one, we thought we’d revisit the full rankings and just give a quick assessment of the year went for each player, what improvements they made, or still need to make, and whether their prospect stock is trending up, down, or neutral as the offseason begins.

Most of the players in this ground from the 21st spot to the 30th spot are 40+ FV prospects. Izaac Pacheco, at 30, is the only one from the 40 FV tier in this article. You can find the full prospect list, with links to each individual scouting report right here. Once again, this is just a look back at the preseason grades and rankings, so players added during the season either in trade or via the draft, aren’t included.

21- RHP Dylan Smith

One of the more surprising DFA decisions of the Tigers season came right as they set their Opening Day roster and decided to put this 25-year-old right-handed reliever on waivers, ultimately trading him to the Giants for cash considerations. Smith went on to throw 39.2 innings for the Giants, collecting four saves while blowing five, with a 3.86 ERA and a 3.63 FIP on the year, good for 0.5 fWAR. That’s about as much as they could’ve hoped for when they dealt for Smith. He doesn’t have closer caliber stuff, and wouldn’t crack the setup man level for many teams.

We’re not going to lose a ton of sleep over a middle reliever with modest ability to handle a setup role, but right-handers like that were in rather short supply for the Tigers at multiple points during the 2026 season. Just a strange bit of roster mismanagement perhaps indicating some overconfidence in their bullpen depth back in March. Smith’s fourseam-slider combination was effective enough for a solid strikeout rate with the Giants and he limited home runs, but some of that is probably related to Oracle Park being a difficult place to hit homers, as Smith allowed a much higher fly ball percentage than he did in the minors. There may have been an element of pitching to the park as well. He still needs to command both pitches more consistently and limit walks to move into regular high leverage setup work, but he took a pretty nice step in his first full year in the major leagues.

Stock: Neutral

22- RHP Ty Madden

Ty Madden spent years in the Tigers system trying to overcome a fourseam fastball with mediocre shape and declining velocity. His command developed pretty nicely considering the deep pitch mix he wields, but some of his issues have never been fully worked out. The club’s competitive balance pick in Round A back in 2021, much was expected of Madden at the time, and very little has been produced. He made a short debut in 2024 and then missed the 2025 season with a rotator cuff injury. Heading into his age 26 season, we still held out hope that Madden would provide some value in relief.

His pre-injury velocity did not fully come back, but Madden thrived pretty well anyway, utilizing his deep pitch mix more effectively in 2026. It took him some time to get on track at Triple-A, but he eventually started finding his groove and eventually threw 46 innings of middle relief for the Tigers with a 3.26 ERA and a 3.55 FIP combination. Putting a 40+ grade on him was a bit ambitious coming back from major shoulder issues, but Madden lived up to the billing. He knows how to pitch and has learned to mix fourseamers, sinkers, and cutters to take pressure off the fourseamer. With a good slider and a decent splitter and knuckle curve, Madden has the arsenal of a starter, but the pitchability of a potentially valuable middle reliever who can handle going through an order multiple times.

I’m not sure there’s much left to squeeze out of his game at this point. The high 90’s velocity he had as a premier college starter has faded a bit, and unless some radical development occurs, this is probably pretty close to his level. The Tigers have been trying to build more ride into the fourseamer for years, and despite a little higher arm slot this year it’s still pretty mediocre action on it. Still, as the first year after a pretty major injury, it was a success. If Madden can get back to his old consistency with his breaking stuff and punch out more hitters nex year, he’ll be even better equipped to handle a mix of longer relief work along with some setup opportunities. It’s just a pretty similar profile to Drew Anderson’s likely position in the bullpen.

Stock: Neutral

23. RHP Michael Massey

Wake Forest alum Michael Massey might be the best pure relief arm in the Tigers’ system. They drafted him in the 4th round of the 2024 draft, and then watched him follow so many of the Tigers top pitchers drafted onto the injury list in his first year of pro ball. After missing all that time for Tommy John surgery and rehab, all we really wanted this year was to see him back on the mound. We got that much as Massey made two short starts late in the year.

Happily, the stuff is still really good. Massey was steadily 94-95 mph with over seven feet of extension to the plate. His most notable quality is the enormous riding action on that fastball due to his high arm slot and release, and that returned intact as well. He averaged nearly 20 inches of induced vertical break, and while we’d love to see him build up to 97-98 mph over the next year or two, the movement and extension makes this a plus fastball already with good potential for more.

The six-foot-five, 230 pounder has the frame to keep building velocity into his mid-20’s. His curveball is another plus pitch, pairing really well with the heater out of Massey’s high arm slot. He packs a pretty good slider as well. Now the challenge is to stay healthy in 2027, build up his arm, and get on with refining his command. That high arm slot requires him to clear his head off the target line a little early, and timing that up can be tricky, but he has the athleticism to make it work. Massey should move very quickly as long as the Tigers develop him as a reliever as expected.

Until we see him settle in for a full season and improve his strike-throwing, we’ll hold him with a 40+ grade, but he has really high end potential in the bullpen. If the velocity and command develop as projected, Massey could be a closing option for the Tigers down the road. The only goal in 2026 was just to get back on the mound. We’ll see where things go from there.

Stock: Neutral

24- C/1B Eduardo Valencia

We were very impressed with Valencia’s breakout at the plate in 2025, but it was still hard to envision a regular role for him with the Tigers, limiting his upside. A decidedly bat first player with a good approach, letting fastballs travel and taking them the opposite way while turning on and crushing breaking balls and changeups, there was a lot to like coming into 2026, and Valencia proved the breakout was real with a really nice major league debut. He hit 8 homers in 42 games while batting .341 and coming up with plenty of big knocks along the way. There was plenty of good fortune on balls in play, and I don’t think Valencia is going to be a consistent .300 hitter, but he is dangerous and kept the strikeouts in check fairly well. If he can be a little more selective in his swing decisions, he should remain a very productive hitter.

The really interesting part of his season was the improvements behind the plate. I still don’t love him as a second catcher, as teams are running more and Valencia’s arm is pretty stretched behind the plate. On the other hand, his framing, blocking, and game calling were all improved to roughly average levels after an impressive offseason’s work. Coming into the season I thought we might have just have a pinch-hitting specialist who could possibly improve as a first baseman but wouldn’t end up catching that much. Instead, Valencia turned himself into a more viable backup to Dillon Dingler and also showed leadership ability and a knack for the big moment. His teammates really seemed to rally around him at times.

Those defensive improvements really help the profile, and bump him up a full grade as he graduates from the system. Valencia is not really built to be an everyday player, but as a backup catcher who will get a lot of plate appearances in the DH slot, he’s got a regular role carved out for himself next year.

Stock: Up

25- RHP Rayner Castillo

This 22-year-old sinkerballer made a fairly impressive full season debut in Single-A back in 2024, but hasn’t been able to take the next steps to break into the upper minors. That’s not surprising considering his age, but now we have back-to-back years with only minor progress. Castillo has a smooth, easy delivery that was steadily producing a tough mid-90’s sinker in 2024 and 2025, but the secondary pitches were still behind the curve. He had a tough go again for parts of this season, but eventually the slider started rounding into form. Just as the strikeouts started to pile up late in the year, he was knocked out in a rough start on September 1 and was shut down at 87.1 innings.

Castillo projected as a future depth starter with possible mid-rotation upside due to his youth and raw stuff. His slider improved this year, but his command of the slider and changeup was still pretty spotty. Still, it’s the glimpses of easy mid-90’s velocity, nasty sink, and high ground ball rate that make him a name worth watching. The fastball command should continue to improve, and he’s still young enough to be optimistic about his secondary pitches becoming more trustworthy weapons. The Tigers may have a pretty good starting pitcher here in time. So, we’ll hold him around this level with a 40+ grade and see if he can put it together and conquer High-A in 2027.

Stock: Neutral

26- OF Brett Callahan

We were higher on Callahan than most in 2024-2025 as he battled a litany of small injuries. Heading into 2026, he finally got some national love and some overcompensated for being late on him by getting a bit too excited. He did reward our confidence in his all around game with a strong campaign at Double-A Erie before leaping quickly through Triple-A to reach the major leagues. Unfortunately, his free swinging ways continued and Callahan got himself out a lot by chasing. As a result, he didn’t tap into his above average raw power much at all after hitting 12 homers in 60 games at Double-A in the first half.

Callahan is a well rounded player, but whether he can lay off chase pitches enough to contribute offensively remains an open question. His rapid trajectory to the majors this year certainly pressed the issue, but he made no progress in his swing decisions. The leap in pitching was just too much for him as he put up a chase rate of 40.1 percent and didn’t make much hard contact. That isn’t sustainable at the big league level, but he didn’t get much time to acclimate himself either. My sense is that Callahan was a little overwhelmed by the rapid promotions and just never settled in after leaving Erie.

The now 25-year-old needs to adapt and improve his approach significantly to get better pitches to hit. If he does, he should do enough damage to earn regular playing time, as the rest of his game is pretty solid, but it’s just a depth outfielder profile unless he can take that big step in 2027. Expect Callahan to work out of Toledo next season while the Tigers see what they have left in Kerry Carpenter and Parker Meadows. That will give him time to work on his approach, and opportunities to get back to the majors will be his for the taking if he can improve.

Stock: Neutral

27- OF Jackson Strong

Another small college outfielder like Callahan, the 23-year-old Strong is developing into a good center fielder, but there are plenty of issues with the hit tool as well. He has some pop and good speed, and does a decent job controlling the strike zone and taking his walks. He hit 17 homers and stole 22 bases for the High-A West Michigan Whitecaps this season while walking a whopping 15.6 percent of the time and playing a pretty nice center field. Unfortunately, he also swings and misses a lot even in the zone, and that was the issue we were looking for improvement with this season. Instead, he struck out nearly 30 percent of the time.

Strong is still working with a fairly grooved swing. He’s a low ball hitter who struggles to cover the upper half of the zone, and is often caught chasing breaking balls and changeups as he hunts for pitches down in the zone. He does show flashes of above average power, but getting to more of it as he progresses is going to be difficult with a lot of chase and too many whiffs as well. The learning curve is steeper for small college hitters who didn’t see much high level stuff, which was part of the pitch for patience with Strong last year. Even so, there aren’t too many hitters who break through and become major league regulars after punching out this much in A-ball.

His speed and defensive ability certainly give him a clean path to an eventual big league role, but the bat has a lot of catching up to do to carry him that far. We gave Strong some benefit of the doubt last spring, and it just didn’t come together. He’s still young enough to wait on, but it got harder to buy into Strong’s bat this year. Even so, legit center fielders with power don’t grow on trees, so the Tigers will have plenty of patience with him.

Stock: Down

28- RHP Moises Rodriguez

This 24-year-old right-hander has a nasty sinker that sometimes touches triple digits. One of the few really interesting pure relief prospects in the system, Rodriguez entered the season at Double-A in need of better command of both the sinker and his slider and unfortunately didn’t make any real progress. He still racked up a massive ground ball rate just shy of 59 percent and rarely allows any home runs, but it remains a difficult profile to float without better command of the sinker. I’d like to see him add some muscle and improve his lower half stability this offseason and hopefully become more consistent in spotting it to both sides of the plate. He’s still an interesting relief option who could develop into something like prime Jason Foley, but while he posted a 2.57 ERA in making the jump to Double-A, there just aren’t enough whiffs in the profile to project much of a major league career if can’t make that happen.

Stock: Down

29- CF Seth Stephenson

After finally conquering High-A with a 2025 season that saw Stephenson make notable improvements in his batspeed and tap into more power, it looked like his contact and speed game had finally gotten the needed boost. Instead, Stephenson struck out more in his first full season at the Double-A level and the power dried up completely. He missed a little time to injury in May, tore it up in June upon his return, but then really faded again in July and August. He did steal 66 bases, illustrating the traits that keep him an interesting young player at a point where the game seems to be valuing speed and contact more highly again. The Eastern League limited pickoff throws to just one this year, and Stephenson and teammate Peyton Graham took full advantage.

There’s still a chance for a Chandler Simpson type player who sprays the ball around and uses his feet to help him hit for average. The problem is that after doing a lot better job of it at the High-A level last year, Stephenson stopped catching balls solidly out in front of the plate and was back in slap and dash mode for most of the year. Most of his fly balls were either pop-ups or routine flyouts where he’s a little late. Getting to even decent gap power looks less likely now, and while his top shelf speed makes him an above average center fielder, Stephenson’s route running and closing ability remain rough around the edges. There’s a role for this type of player but only if he can start driving better pitching more often next year. He’ll be 26 in January, so further progress needs to come quickly.

Stock: Down

30- 3B/1B Izaac Pacheco

Pacheco was the one player in this group with a 40 grade last offseason. After four straight years trying to break out of the High-A level, the slugging third baseman finally managed a much improved season in 2025 and got himself back on the radar to a degree. Unfortunately, all the same issues reared their heads at the Double-A level. His power potential remains enormous, and he did a little better job getting to it this season, hitting 24 home runs, 21 of them at the Double-A level. On the other hand, better pitching carved him up routinely as Pacheco posted a brutal 33.9 percent strikeout rate. After years of adjustments and swing changes, he’s tapping into his power at the bottom of the zone but still struggles to cover the rest of the plate with any real consistency even against fastballs. There are just so many comfortable ways for better pitchers to get him out while avoiding Pacheco’s sweet spots in the strike zone.

One saving grace is that his defense at the corners is actually pretty solid. He’s more than a future possible DH. There’s still a pathway to the major leagues for Pacheco, but it remains very narrow. He’s refined his swing and approach to hit a lot of fly balls to the pull field specifically because he has to maximize the damage on his limited amounts of hard contact. To carry that approach to the majors, he’s got to become more selective in his swing decisions. This three true outcomes type of hitting profile is rapidly disappearing around the game, and only players with a great eye for doing damage, like Munetaka Murakami, are really making it work. Pacheco will turn 24 in two weeks, so he really needs to make some adjustments and conquer upper level pitching next season or he’ll be left behind as the next waves of Tigers prospects pass him by.

Stock: Down
